cards.title: Two ways to steepen a yield curve
cards.prompt: Can a yield curve steepen while both short and long yields fall? Explain using a long–short spread.
cards.answer:
A curve steepens when the long–short yield spread increases. Both yields may rise, both may fall, or they may move in opposite directions. These hypothetical points illustrate the distinction.

cards.title: Duration gap and the insurer's surplus
cards.prompt: Why does matching asset and liability duration in years alone fail when their values differ?
cards.answer:
A balance-sheet duration gap compares value-weighted interest-rate exposure. In this first-order parallel-shock model, surplus sensitivity depends on A × Dₐ − L × Dₗ, not simply Dₐ − Dₗ.

cards.title: Weak references, ownership and cleanup
cards.prompt: Does closing a resource or storing a weak reference guarantee its wrapper is collected? Trace the strong owners.
cards.answer:
A weak reference observes an object without keeping it alive. Closing a resource releases its handle; collection depends on reachability. A caller that saves the result of a live weak-reference read creates a temporary strong owner.

```widget Weak references, ownership and cleanup

Reachability, made visible

A reference is not always an owner.

Closing a resource and collecting its wrapper are different events. Trace the strong paths before running GC.

Simplified reachability trace, not a promise about GC timing or process RSS. A live weakref call returns the object; storing that result keeps a strong reference until the caller releases it.

```
